summary: Defines a MIB module for the reverse direction of RFC 5675: turning syslog messages into SNMP notifications. A management system can then receive syslog events as SNMP traps. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: This is the translation guide going the other way. A note written in a log diary can be turned into a loud alert message that a network manager's tools already know how to hear.

subtitle: How a syslog collector can store log messages as SNMP objects and send them on as SNMP notifications.

tldr.problem: Some environments want all event notifications collected through one protocol, but events arrive as both SYSLOG messages and SNMP notifications.
tldr.mechanism: A SYSLOG-to-SNMP translator parses each syslog message, records its fields in two MIB tables, and may send an SNMP notification carrying them.
tldr.outcome: SNMP tools can read recent syslog messages and receive them as notifications, and the mapping pairs with RFC 5675 for the opposite direction.

today: RFC 5676 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2009. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It pairs with RFC 5675, which covers the opposite direction.

sections.title: Why Translate Syslog to SNMP
sections.content:
SNMP and SYSLOG (RFC 5424) are two widely used ways to communicate event notifications. Some environments need all events collected by a single system, either a SYSLOG collector or an SNMP notification receiver, through one management protocol. That requires translating between the two.

RFC 5676 defines an SNMP MIB module, SYSLOG-MSG-MIB, that represents SYSLOG messages and sends them as SNMP notifications. It is registered as { mib-2 192 }.
sections.eli5: If one friend writes notes and another only listens for shouts, someone has to turn the notes into shouts. This document says how.

sections.title: How the Translator Works
sections.content:
A SYSLOG-to-SNMP translator acts as a SYSLOG collector and implements the MIB module. It may be tightly coupled to an SNMP agent or talk to one through a subagent protocol.

After initialization it listens for SYSLOG messages. For each one it parses out the fields, fills a conceptual table, and may then generate a notification. Two scalars control this: syslogMsgTableMaxSize limits how many messages are kept (0 means no fixed limit, and the default is 0), and syslogMsgEnableNotifications turns notifications on or off (default false). If the table limit is lowered, the messages held longest MUST be discarded.
sections.eli5: The translator sits by a mailbox of log notes, copies each one into a tidy notebook, and, if the switch is on, shouts about it.

sections.title: The Two Tables
sections.content:
syslogMsgTable has one entry per recorded message, indexed by syslogMsgIndex. Its columns are facility, severity, version, timestamp, host name, app name, procid, msgid, the number of structured data parameters, and the message text. The index wraps back to 1 after reaching 4294967295.

syslogMsgSDTable holds one entry per structured data element parameter. Because structured data is optional, a message has from zero to many entries here. Entries are indexed by message index, a parameter index (which counts across element boundaries), the SD-ID and the parameter name, and the value is stored unescaped.

Where a field is unknown the MIB uses a marker: version 0, or a zero-length string for timestamp, host name, app name, procid and msgid. The message text may be truncated to fit the implementation, and if it starts with the octets EFBBBF the rest is UTF-8.
sections.eli5: One notebook holds a line for each message. A second notebook holds the extra labeled details attached to a message, if there are any.

sections.title: The Notification and Combining with RFC 5675
sections.content:
The syslogMsgNotification is generated when a new SYSLOG message is received and notifications are enabled. It carries facility, severity, version, timestamp, host name, app name, procid, msgid, the structured data parameter count and the message. Implementations may add syslogMsgSDParamValue objects if the result fits the size limits.

The companion RFC 5675 maps SNMP notifications to SYSLOG messages. Used together, the two allow chains where notifications are tunneled through the other protocol. A notification can be truncated by SYSLOG size limits. When tunneling SYSLOG through SNMP, a forwarder that sees missing structured data parameters MUST fetch them from the MIB, and regular polling can cover lost notifications.

Three compliance statements exist: full, read-only (write access not required for the two control objects) and notification-only (no table read access needed).
sections.eli5: When a new log note arrives, the translator can send a short alert with the main details. If something was left out, the receiver can look it up in the notebook.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Two objects are writable. Changing syslogMsgTableMaxSize without authorization could raise memory use, or set it to zero and stop retrieval of notifications, which might hide traces of an attack. Disabling syslogMsgEnableNotifications can hide an attack from real-time monitoring, and enabling it could support a denial-of-service attack on the management system if the translator accepts unauthorized SYSLOG messages.

The message objects carry syslog content, so the security considerations of RFC 5424 apply, and SNMP access control should enforce a consistent policy. The RFC RECOMMENDS SNMPv3 with cryptographic security and says deploying earlier SNMP versions is NOT RECOMMENDED. SNMPv3 protects only the SNMP leg, so deployments should also use SYSLOG security mechanisms to stop attackers adding malicious data.
sections.eli5: Log notes can contain secrets and the switches can hide trouble, so only trusted people should be allowed to read the notebook or flip the switches.
